Deep-learning techniques such as Sequence-to-Sequence networks, LSTMs and GRUs that are used to forecast business processes have seen significant improvement in recent years. However, there is little research that compares these methods to determine which one is most effective for various processes. Most current studies show that there is significant variability in the data related to accounting processes. To address this issue, this study compares the forecasting accuracy of four deep-learning techniques including Multi-Layer Percetron, LSTMs, GRUs and SS networks to determine which one is most effective for variable business processes. The findings of this research which used real data from an Italian company for six different financial performance indicators over a two-year period show that there is no significant difference in the forecasting accuracy of LSTMs and GRUs to predict regular processes, whereas for noisy processes, GRUs are more accurate than LSTMs. Additionally, both LSTMs and GRUs are more accurate than SS networks in forecasting noisy processes, whereas for regular processes, SS networks are more accurate than both LSTMs and GRUs. The results of this research can be utilized by company managers to select the most effective deep-learning technique for forecasting regular and noisy business processes. Furthermore, the findings of this research along with the dataset and code can be used as a platform for other researchers to conduct further comparison of different deep-learning techniques for forecasting business processes. This research also highlights the importance of process variability for different financial performance indicators and presents policy recommendations related to this issue. Lastly, this research proposes a model to reduce noise in business processes which can be utilized by other researchers as a baseline model. An enormous eruption of 1000 times stellar luminosity occurred for AD Leo in 1985 April, primarily emitting energy in the near-ultraviolet, where the number of available continuum models is limited. To study this event, we developed a new method for determining the relative contributions of different UV components in dwarf stars by examining ratios of various spectral lines. This approach allowed us to investigate the onset of giant eruptions in dwarf stars and the behavior of their outer atmospheres. By analyzing these ratios, we determined the relative contributions of the stellar surface, hot layers, and outer space in AD Leo's spectrum both normally and during the massive eruption of 1985. Our results show that the eruption significantly increased the contribution of helium lines originating from the outer space, as well as the amount of continued stellar energy being absorbed by space. Additionally, we found that the atmosphere of AD Leo is more active than generally believed, with some characteristics persisting even after the eruption. Based on these findings, we propose that the massive eruption of 1985 was caused by a massive flaring star, and we suggest that most eruptions of this type may have similar causes. Furthermore, we observe that the activity persisted even after the massive eruption of 1985, causing us to suggest that the behavior of dwarf stars during these events may have been previously misinterpreted. Our research was conducted using data from the IUE satellite, specifically the long-wavelength UV spectrum covering the wavelength range 2000-3000 Angstroms, and our results are consistent with a recent analysis of another massive eruption that occurred in 1992 July. Our work may have implications for understanding the levels of pre-eruptive and post-eruptive activity in dwarf stars, as well as the duration of these eruptions, and provides a new perspective on the famous massive eruption that occurred in 1992 July in the SY Cep system. Our findings also suggest that the coronal temperature of dwarf stars remains constant, and that the massive eruptions of these stars are caused by the release of accumulated energy rather than the instantaneous effects of flares. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another through panspermia, potentially originating from interstellar space, is both captivating and complex. While this concept is intriguing, it's also challenging to assess, given the uncertain nature of biogenic signals and the lack of a clear method to determine their interstellar source. To address this, we must consider how specifically interstellar panspermia can be distinguished from similar phenomena that might arise within a system due to its own life and death processes, such as microbial life forming on comets or meteorites or microorganisms being discharged into space as part of the death processes of stars. To explore this, we evaluated existing and hypothetical signals that could indicate panspermia, analyzing their credibility and how easily they could be confused with natural astrophysical processes. Animal population studies often aim to understand how animals interact with their environment and select habitats.  Traditional methods of analyzing capture-recapture data primarily focus on quantifying population size.  However, such data contain historical records of locations and times of animal captures, potentially offering a wealth of information about habitat use.  Recently, models have been developed to incorporate capture-recapture data into statistical estimates of population size and density while accounting for habitat selection behavior.  These models use detection probabilities for capture-recapture data and express these in terms of density and habitat selection parameters.  By applying capture-recapture methods on a large scale, researchers can obtain precise estimates of these detection probabilities.  This paper presents novel analytical tools to analyze capture-recapture data from multi-camera traps.  Each camera is associated with a specific area within the environment, allowing for the collection of choice data as animals selectively use certain cameras over others.  By integrating capture-recapture data from multiple cameras with the same capture location, we can distinguish between the areas associated with high or low density and refine our estimates of habitat selection parameters.  The capture-recapture models presented in this paper incorporate choice data directly, eliminating the need for choice models.  The paper also presents a novel Bayesian approach to analyze capture-recapture data and forecasts expected detection probabilities for unseen locations.  This research was conducted in the state of Maine where biologists are managing deer populations through controlled hunting.  The aim of this study was to investigate habitat selection behavior of deer in a spatial context and to develop predictive models of detection probabilities for capture-recapture estimates of density.  The results show that models based on capture-recapture data alone provide accurate estimates of detection probabilities and therefore reliable inferences about habitat selection behavior.  The paper also presents a statistical approach to analyze capture-recapture data and forecasts expected detection probabilities for unseen locations. Large-scale network estimation tasks, such as calculating a sum or an average, are common in distributed systems and can be challenging to achieve accurately, especially when the network contains unreliable nodes that provide false information. In this research, we examine the possibility of accurately estimating a network's global sum or average within a small-world graph, assuming that the majority of the network consists of trustworthy nodes and there are only a few malicious nodes contributing to the errors. By analyzing the effects of both random and deliberate errors, we establish lower bounds for the accuracy of these estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under certain conditions, reliable average (RA) and small-world reliable average (SWRA) algorithms can achieve the minimum error threshold asynchronously. To demonstrate the applicability of these results, we also explore specific small-world graph scenarios, such as random graph models. If the graph is structured and deterministic, with a fixed and known structure, we can design efficient algorithms that match the minimum error threshold. Additionally, for certain dynamic and probabilistic random graph models, we identify specific parameters that ensure the minimum error threshold is maintained. If the network is structured and deterministic, with a node degree of at least three, we can achieve the minimum error threshold through a two-round protocol. In contrast, for the dynamic and probabilistic random graph models, with a node degree of two, we find that the minimum error threshold cannot be maintained, indicating that these models are insufficiently robust for network scale estimation tasks. In the case of reliable average, if the node degree is two, we find that the algorithm requires at least three rounds to achieve the minimum error threshold. In the context of small-world reliable average, if the node degree is two, we find that the algorithm requires a much longer period of time (proportional to the square of the network size) to achieve the minimum error threshold, indicating that this model is highly sensitive to errors and requires additional graph connectivity improvements to function efficiently. In the case of random graph models, we examine the relationship between the accuracy of these algorithms and the two key dimensions of random graph models: the node degree and the switching probability. Our analysis shows that there is a positive, albeit slow, rate at which the accuracy of these algorithms increases as the node degree increases, whereas the effect of changing the switching probability has a more complex impact on the accuracy, depending on the specific distribution of the graph. Our research also enables us to identify various randomized small-world graph scenarios that are resistant to the deterioration of average estimation accuracy. In this study, we investigate the magnetic properties and the Nernst effect of Mn$_3$NiN (100) thin films, focusing on the effects of temperature and layer thickness. A notable phenomenon, the Nernst dip, is observed in thick manganese nickel nitride films, unlike the experimental outcome for the bulk material. Yet, this film's Nernst effect shows a significant change with temperature and layer thickness, indicating the Nernst dip's sensitivity to interface scattering. Moreover, we find that the conventional Eddy current damping's contribution is crucial for accurately describing the Nernst effect. On the other hand, the minimal model is adequate for describing the magnetic properties. This concept finds expression in the paradox of Achilles and a tortoise, commonly attributed to Greek philosopher Zeno. Although this paradox is often seen as a classic example of a logical obstacle, it can alternatively be viewed as a genuine reflection of the limitations it poses on a particular theoretical framework. To understand this alternative perspective, a brief examination of the paradox through the lenses of both ancient and modern philosophical frameworks is necessary. Our study utilizes a multiphase transport model to simulate Pb-Pb collisions, with the goal of accurately determining collective flow parameters relying on event shape variables. We investigate how events are selected and sorted to exhibit varying levels of elliptic flow patterns, and examine four commonly employed event shape variables: the fourth order flow coefficient, the eccentricity of the collision system, the multiplicity distribution, and the algebraic sum of the flow angles. Our findings show that selected event shapes are unbiased with regard to charge distribution, and thus elliptic flow parameters are unaffected by charge arrangement. We also determine the relationship between initial state conditions and collective flow, and show that selected event shapes exhibit distinct asymmetries in x-y and $\phi$ distributions. A significant issue in legged robot locomotion is the uncertainty that arises when navigating through diverse terrain conditions. This research focuses on simulating and improving a single-legged jumping robot as it moves over different types of soft terrain, particularly soft foam layers of varying thickness. The project aims to explore the potential for robots to leap over challenges by incorporating a protective layer, and we study the effects of different plate spring model variables, as well as the impact of adding a muscle-spinal cord model-based control system, on the robot's movement. Our findings reveal that an optimal layer thickness exists for each movement speed, our demonstration of a muscle-spinal cord model shows that controlled landing is possible, and we successfully implemented a safe landing through a controlled lean, thereby minimizing the force of impact. Our findings have been published in separate papers, and all simulation data have been made available via the website "http://runner.steveyang.org/foam". This work was supported by the Creative Research Initiative of the Office of Academic Research, SNU, and the National Science Foundation.

Hierarchies in information systems, stemming from the principle of information diminishment, follow a natural progression from specific to general information. They exhibit a distinct property where each higher-level concept is inherently inclusive of its corresponding lower-level concept. This property serves as the basis for our proposed expansion in the context of information systems models. We outline how this property can be expressed through the use of predicates and describe a standard format for concept hierarchies. We also clarify what we mean by expandable models and identify those that satisfy this condition. Furthermore, we establish a key theorem demonstrating that certain hierarchies are indeed programmatically expandable. To accomplish this, we draw upon the principles of first-order logic and the concept of interpretations. The task of calculating with hierarchies in information systems involves making calculations that respect hierarchy relationships, and we illustrate this through a sample examination of the hierarchy $2$.\forallX\subseteq\forall\exists X$. Finally, we provide a brief discussion on the implications of our findings for the community of information system researchers. This research was previously published in the Journal of Applied Non-Classical Logics, volume 27. Conversely, when particle growth is effective, it may suppress VSI, given its ability to resist shear instability caused by friction between particles and gas. In this study, we used numerical modeling with high resolution to examine the effect of particle growth on VSI in a simplified model of a protoplanetary disk. We observed the VSI's transformation from an unstable state to being stable as dust particles grew and developed their own mass through modeling with various gas temperatures and particle sizes. Furthermore, we found that a specific saturation level existed for dust mass structure depth, which was dependent on initial particle sizes and resisted changes with gas temperature. This result is significant because it provides a crucial insight into dust development's role in the VSI's formation, and also demonstrates how VSI's occurrence or absence will be influenced by conditions such as solar energy input, rather than just the amount of particles present. Recently introduced dynamic entrance networks have been shown to be effective in addressing classification challenges that involve multiple tasks. By allocating different data to different tasks, these networks can significantly improve performance. However, the current fixed method of determining task-specific data using a weighted sum does not take into account the inherent differences between various datasets. To address this limitation, this study introduces a novel dynamic entrance framework known as GMP-DEN, which utilizes a weighted sum based on a globally learned distribution of interest. The proposed GMP-DEN encompasses two primary components: the first component identifies the presence of data based on a binary activation function, while the second component determines the degree of interest in the data using a global mean pooling layer. Experimental evaluations conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate improved performance for GMP-DEN compared to fixed entrance networks and alternative dynamic entrance baselines. By leveraging the proposed GMP-DEN, models can be trained to be more robust and adaptable to various classification challenges. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang84/Dynamic-Entrance-Network. The proposed GMP-DEN has been applied to two specific scenarios: single-sample multi-task classification and semi-supervised learning, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets. We are examining the impact of the post-Newtonian gravity parameter $\gamma$ on the measurement of parallaxes, which arises from the change in the apparent position of a star resulting from the motion of the Sun, mainly caused by the non-homogeneity of the gravitational field throughout the Milky Way. To create more realistic chatbots, our model aims to incorporate a feature called semantic connections between questions and answers, which refers to the underlying relationships, connections, and links that provide context and structure to our world of knowledge. To facilitate this, we developed a method to automatically identify and quantify these semantic connections between questions and possible answers. To incorporate these connections into our model, we employed a strategic sampling approach to ensure that our model is exposed to a diverse range of questions with diverse connections to the answer choices. To evaluate this feature, we created a new metric called the connection score, which gauges the semantic connections between questions and answers and provides valuable insights into the degree of structure and context that our model has mastered. To validate our approach, we compared it to alternative methods and found that our method outperforms them according to various criteria, including performance, semantic connections, and explicit common sense reasoning. Furthermore, we discovered that the connections scored by our model align with human-assigned labels that indicate the degree of structure and context in each question, providing valuable insights into the underlying relationships and connections between questions and answers. To ensure that our model has a broad range of common sense, we designed a new challenging evaluation framework called semantic connection barriers, which consists of three levels of increasing difficulty, and demonstrated that our approach consistently ranks higher than the existing state-of-the-art model on this framework. To assess the generality of our approach, we applied it to a different dataset and found that our method successfully transferred to this new dataset and provided a better performance compared to the alternative methods. To create a more realistic chatbot, our model can be trained in a controlled environment for a limited number of rounds, and we recommend using a small set of questions with diverse connections to the answers for this purpose. To this end, we developed a tool called Coarse-to-Careful, which is an open-source interactive learning environment that allows for the controlled training and validation of our model, and provides a visual interface to visualize the semantic connections between questions and answers, as well as interactive tools to exchange messages between questions and answers, and to validate the context and structure of our model. A pervasive issue in healthcare image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new technique to extend semi-supervised image segmentation models to achieve better performance when only provided with rough sketch-style annotations. This technique, known as consistency regularization using basic models for supervised learning, relies on simple neural networks to ensure the consistency of sketch annotations. This consistency ensures that the annotations align with the segmentation outputs generated by the model when given more detailed annotations. By applying this technique, we develop a method that can be used in conjunction with existing models and datasets. This method demonstrates its value in multiple healthcare image segmentation scenarios. When compared to multiple baseline models, our technique consistently achieves comparable results when only provided with 5% detailed annotations. Furthermore, this technique can be combined with existing transfer learning methods,, including the use of pre-trained models based on contrastive learning, to achieve even better performance. This is evident in our experiments, which show that our technique leads to segmentations that are more accurate and comprehensive, even when only provided with 5% detailed annotations. This is achievable in multiple healthcare image segmentation scenarios, including the analysis of abdominal organs and the segmentation of tumors from medical images. Our technique, which is simple and efficient, provides a step-by-step guide on how to integrate it with existing models and datasets. This guide includes the creation of basic neural networks, as well as the optimization of model parameters to achieve the best results. Our code and additional information about this technique are available online at https://github.com/ghrua/Basic-Consistency-Regulation-Technique. This technique can be used by researchers working on healthcare image segmentation tasks and anyone else interested in the application of consistency regularization using basic models for supervised learning. This paper is accompanied by an accompanying video that depicts a 3D reconstruction of a heart model derived from image segmentation. This reconstruction was achieved using the technique introduced in this paper. This video along with the code and additional information about this technique are available online at https://sites.google.com/view/basic-consistency-regulation. Complex dynamics in many-body systems pose significant challenges in predicting long-term behavior due to limited knowledge of initial conditions and fluctuations in subsequent developments. For such systems, where full stability cannot be ensured, small changes in initial conditions can significantly impact the outcome, leading to incomplete results when analyzing dynamics. A new framework is introduced that uses graph neural networks to determine the sensitivity of these systems by plotting the relationship between initial conditions and subsequent dynamics. This connection is presented as a graph showing the variation in values over time, providing a clear visual representation of how different initial conditions influence the outcome. As a test case, this framework is applied to a simple, chaotic model known as the logistic map, as well as a many-body chaotic system based on the Rydberg molecular interaction, allowing for an intuitive understanding of how tiny changes in initial conditions affect the outcome in these systems. By converting complex time series data into an easily interpretable graph format, this framework offers a practical solution for analyzing the sensitivity of many-body systems, as well as other dynamics where initial conditions are uncertain. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghulam-saqib/Graph-NeuralNetwork-ChaoticDynamics. Given an open and affine variety $X$, we demonstrate that there is a finite generating set $S$ for the polynomial ring $k[X]$, such that for any linear differential operator $P$, there exists a polynomial $Q$ with which satisfies the relationship $\sqrt{\frac{\partial^d}{\partial X^d} Q} \bigl(\frac{\partial^d}{\partial X^d})^{d-1}$ divides $\bigl(\frac{\partial^d}{\partial X^d} P \bigr) \bigl(\frac{\partial^d}{\partial X^d})^{d-1}$ for all degrees $d$. This implies that the set of coefficients in the differential operator $P$ has a specific range and is defined as the collection of coefficients in polynomials of the form $f^{d!}Q$, where $f \in k[X]$ and $Q \in k[S]$. This in turn leads to the conclusion that the ring $k[X][\frac{\partial}{\partial X}]$ is not faithful as a module over the ring $k[X][t]$. Furthermore, this result extends to rings that are Euclidean extensions and shows that systems of differential operators can be regarded as a specific type of analytic systems of operators, for which a result from the paper "Analytic systems of operators and their applications" is established, where it is shown that there are no systems of differential operators that are faithful as modules over the polynomial ring in the variable $t$. Lastly, this result also implies that there are no universal differential operators that are faithful as modules over the polynomial ring in the variable $t$, which in turn leads to the conclusion that there are no universal differential operators of the form $\Delta^d$ for the purpose of approximating the ring of polynomials. Lastly, this result also implies that there are no differential operators that are equivalent to the derivative operator itself, which in turn leads to the conclusion that there are no universal differential operators of the form $\Delta^d$ for the purpose of approximating the ring of polynomials over such fields and provides a different proof for the result from the paper "On the non-existence of the universal differential operator of the first order over fields of transcendental variables". Creating effective proof-based learning methods for satisfiability moderators requires a standardized framework for presenting and sharing evidence. Yet, different satisfiability moderators, originating from diverse underlying solvers and proof systems, often produce incompatible evidence due to the numerous and conflicting standards for representing proofs. To address this issue and facilitate a seamless exchange of knowledge, we propose Alethe, a versatile format for representing and translating evidence, which can be applied to a broad spectrum of satisfiability moderators, proof systems, and theories. We demonstrate the versatility of this format by illustrating an evidence translation between the Veritas solver and the CVC3 theorem prover. Furthermore, we showcase the utility of this format in integrating learning methods with a range of satisfiability moderators. The Alethe format, its implementation, and example codes are available online at https://alethe.github.io/.

This paper introduces two significant innovations in federated learning with synchronous aggregation. Firstly, we relax the assumption that participants have access to high-quality gradients, by allowing them to submit unconstrained gradient updates. Secondly, we enhance the feasibility of efficient data sampling by allowing participants to enroll in the training process without a prerequisite for pre-allocated anonymous identifiers. To accommodate these advancements, we develop a new algorithm that incorporates buffered aggregation in conjunction with random participant selection. Our proposed method is comparable to existing techniques and outperforms them in unconstrained settings. Our research showcases that fedlearn and floren are overoptimistic models and suggests alternatives for their future improvement. Moreover, we demonstrate that unconstrained gradients and buffered aggregation in conjunction with random participant selection are interchangeable, resulting in fedlearn being an excessive model. Lastly, our research publishes unconstrained gradient descent as the standard benchmark, resulting in fedlearn's first-ever loss improvement. Our experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, indicating that it is a versatile technique with widespread applications. Our research is applicable to a broad range of unsupervised and supervised learning tasks, including classification, regression, and topic modeling. Our proposed algorithm has been made available online for public use. Our research highlights potential paths for future innovation in fedlearn, random participant selection, and unconstrained gradients, all of which are available at https://github.com/happy-song/fedbuf. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome these challenges by utilizing existing knowledge from a related task. Two aspects of transfer learning in ASR are explored in this paper. First, we investigate performing a coarse-to-fine recognition process where a initial classification is made on a less precise task, followed by further refinement on a more detailed one. Our results show this approach is effective especially in narrowing down the number of possible outcomes. Second, we look at inter-language transfer in ASR, where the knowledge from one language is used to improve recognition on another. We used a setup with multi-speaker support where knowledge from a combination of Norwegian and Swedish speakers was used to enhance recognition of Danish, our results indicate a 12.57% reduction in word error rate compared to the baseline. Our code has been made available at github.com/ SpeechWave/rl-asr-transfer.

Research in navigation systems for marine robots focuses on combining internal sensors with external signals like radio frequency (RF) transmissions, satellite signals, or ocean currents. Although current navigation systems for marine robots are highly accurate, they can be compromised by signal loss or varying water currents. To address this issue, researchers have explored using model-based methods to estimate navigation systems' performance and identify areas where the signal is missing or the current is varying rapidly. These models typically use statistical techniques to predict performance degradation and treat the variation of water currents as a constant factor. However, existing models do not account for the uncertainty of performance degradation and the changing water currents over time. To improve the accuracy of navigation systems for marine robots, a novel Gaussian Process model has been developed that takes into account the performance's sparsity, the varying water currents, and the accuracy of the navigation system's signals. This model uses a Gaussian Process with a sparse kernel function to model the performance of the navigation system, allows for the estimation of the sparsity of performance, and incorporates a state estimator to track the water currents over time. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, navigation system performance was evaluated in an indoor environment with varying water currents using a robot carrying an RF transmitter, and the results showed that the model accurately predicted performance degradation, the variation of water currents, and the navigation system's accuracy. These findings have important implications for designing and evaluating navigation systems for marine robots, and the model presented here can be used as a tool for researchers and developers working on navigation systems for marine robots. The model's performance was also compared to existing models, and the results revealed that it outperforms them in terms of navigation system accuracy, performance prediction, and the variability of water currents. The model has been implemented on a marine robot navigation system in an outdoor environment with RF transmissions, and the results showed that it can adapt to changing water currents and track the navigation system's performance and signals accurately. These achievements have been recognized through the award of the Best Application Paper at the 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems. The model has also been tested on an underwater navigation system using acoustic transmissions, and the results showed that it can adapt to changing water currents and track the navigation system's performance and signals accurately. The model has been found to be compatible with a variety of navigation systems, including RF and acoustic transmissions, and has been developed into a software package available online. The model has been recognized through the award of the Best Application Paper at the 2022 IEEE/RSJ International

We establish a new approach to examine multi-fluid objects in General Relativity, using a 2-fluid sphere as an example. This approach allows us to explore the relationship between the gravitational field and fluid movement, even in situations where the fluids move at different speeds. By applying this method to a 2-fluid sphere in General Relativity, we derive an equation describing its structure, specifically the equation that describes how the gravitational field changes with distance from the sphere's center. This equation must be solved in conjunction with two separate equation that describe the sphere's structure in the absence of gravity, one for each type of fluid. Although this approach is particularly beneficial for fluids that don't easily resist gravity, such as gases, it also helps us understand the effects of slow fluid movement and gravitational field irregularities on the fluids' behavior. This is especially relevant for dense fluids like liquids, where fluid movement is typically slow. This research was previously published in 2019. The key equation derived from this analysis, the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation, can be used to solve for the sphere's structure in the presence of gravity for each type of fluid, using the method developed in 1937 by Tolman, Oppenheimer, and Volkoff. This is specifically achievable when the distribution of matter within the sphere is uniform. However, if the distribution of matter within the sphere is non-uniform, this approach requires a different solution, specifically the "relativistic Ricci matrix equation". This research provides an alternative way of examining non-uniform celestial bodies in General Relativity, and shows that any change in the distribution of matter within the sphere always results in a change in the sphere's structure over time, even in the absence of gravity. Evaluating grammatical errors in languages is a critical step before translating or summarizing text. Despite the importance of this task, reliable reference datasets are scarce, making it challenging to apply state-of-the-art machine learning models in this domain. This paper introduces a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, to tackle the limited data constraint and enable model domain transfer capability. We demonstrate a model's capability to acquire the rules of a target domain by combining a core model with a little data, and show that it can effectively adapt to new domains with limited examples. The proposed method achieves superior performance in five target domains when compared to a baseline model, and further improves upon itself when evaluating domain-specific semantic errors. Additionally, the model exhibits versatility in handling both collective and incremental domain adaptations. To validate the proposed method on a broader scale, we also conduct additional experiments using a publicly available dataset, with both small and large target domains. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SOFT-GER.

It has also been found that, for many integrity constraints, certain common distributive sequences do result in pure Nash equilibria that are fair and equitable when the number of agents is greater than two. A key aspect of these distributive sequences is that they solely incorporate local rules based on the relationship between agents and the available goods, and do not rely on complex knowledge requirements from the agent's part. Moreover, these distributive sequences can be seen as a specific instance of a broader concept called potential function, which has significant implications for understanding the complex relationship between fairness, equity, and stability in multi-agent settings. Evaluating the range of accretion rates among T Tauri stars is crucial for understanding the distinct processes that T Tauri stars undergo. An elevated level of accretion is believed to cause magnetic reconnection, resulting in X-ray emission, while a lower level of accretion gives rise to irregular bursts of X-ray emission resulting from magnetic shear. However, the accuracy of these assumptions may be compromised by the limited amount of data available. The observations of XX Cha, a T Tauri star, revealed unusual and persistent high-frequency fluctuations in X-ray emission, as well as a narrow range of accretion rates over the course of nine years. These findings are exceptional among documented T Tauri stars and indicate that the range of accretion rates in XX Cha is the lowest recorded to date. Additionally, the persistent high-frequency fluctuations in XX Cha are similar to the variations in X-ray emission observed from the dwarf nova, DQ Herculis during its quiescent state. The generalized relationship between accretion rates and the character of X-ray emission also supports the idea that XX Cha falls within the category of T Tauri stars that exhibit irregular X-ray bursts as a result of low-level accretion and magnetic shear. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to the presence of opposing actions, such as actions that degrade the environment and harm the system, since many past experiences may not be beneficial for current tasks. This paper focuses on learning from positive past trajectories, assuming there are few completely adverse actions. We introduce a new model, Positive Trajectory Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PT-MARL), which draws upon the strengths of cooperative and competitive methods. PT-MARL uses a combination of forward learning to capture beneficial actions and backward learning to identify adverse ones. By using a distinct structure of policy networks for each other, we enable the model to distinguish between interacting agents and system components. This allows for better utilization of positive past experiences and enhances the robustness of the system. Experimental results on various offline datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing that PT-MARL outperforms multiple baselines and adaptive opponents. Moreover, we explore the practical application of our method to a complex system involving multiple interacting agents, including a notable example with route planning. Our code is available at https://github.com/hkew/PT-MARL.

The notion that entanglement between two particles is necessary for true nonlocality to arise has been a long-standing misconception. Utilizing the EPR paradox and the GHZ paradox as examples, it can be demonstrated that the nonlocal properties of a single particle are capable of guiding the behavior of another particle at a separate location, regardless of the absence of entanglement between them. In fact, if two particles were connected by EPR scenarios or GHZ scenarios, completing each situation would result in the presence of single-particle nonlocality, yet this would actually diminish the level of nonlocality exhibited. Consequently, a distinction is drawn between single-particle entanglement, single-particle nonlocality, and single-particle steering, with the latter being the genuine nonlocal effect that arises in single-particle scenarios. Additionally, the relationship between these effects and their corresponding relations, as well as their reliance on the particles' initial state, are examined. Lastly, the inclusion of single-particle nonlocality into the genuine nonlocality criteria is proposed, with discussions surrounding its implications.

Countries experiencing high levels of electricity grid disturbance face challenges in developing effective auxiliary services policies to utilize responsive grid assets efficiently. A prevalent issue is the lack of reliable data on grid behavior during extreme events, making it difficult to design suitable auxiliary services policies. In addition, researchers often overlook interactions between sectors and the electricity market in their analysis, which can lead to faulty policy conclusions. This study addresses these limitations by exploring sector-specific and electricity market interactions in a hypothetical case study involving severe disturbances. A novel approach is taken where auxiliary services are viewed as a separate service from load, represented by an own merit in a mixed-integer linear programming model of the electricity market. This results in multiple possible representations of grid behavior during extreme events, from a fully centralized scenario to a decentralized scenario with sector-specific assets. Which representation is most applicable is determined by comparing the consistency of the resulting auxiliary services schedules with historical data on sector-specific loads and market patterns. This consistency is viewed as a measure of sector-specific load's ability to withstand changes in auxiliary services without deviating significantly. A novel auxiliary services procurement model is then developed that accounts for sector-specific load's ability to withstand changes in auxiliary services without deviating significantly. This model enables the accurate representation of grid behavior during extreme events, reducing the risk of flawed policy conclusions. The validity of this model is supported by the results of case studies conducted on the Australian and New Zealand electricity markets. These studies demonstrate that auxiliary services procurement models can be reliable tools in the hands of policymakers, but they require the careful consideration of sector-specific load and electricity market interactions to prevent the risk of flawed policy conclusions. This research also highlights the importance of utilizing responsive grid assets in Australia and New Zealand, which can reduce the need for expensive must-run loads during extreme events. This is particularly evident in the Australian case study, which shows that must-run loads can be reduced from 240 MW to 100 MW in response to the deployment of responsive grid assets. This study provides a novel auxiliary services procurement model that accounts for sector-specific load and electricity market interactions in policy development, presenting an opportunity for researchers and policymakers to explore further the implications of this model on the reliability and efficiency of the electricity grid. This model has been tested on the Australian and New Zealand electricity markets, which have different market structures, but both are characterized by a high level of sectoral autonomy. This research on the Australian and New Zealand electricity markets provides a unique contribution to the global literature on auxiliary services procurement models, which have primarily been tested on emerging markets with limited sectoral autonomy. Our approach creates a unified framework for translating between multiple languages by organizing words into shared semantic clusters, which share equivalent structures across different languages. To accomplish this, we develop a novel method for clustering words and a new evaluation metric that assesses the similarity of language models' cluster structures. Our approach surpasses existing multilingual evaluation metrics and provides a precise assessment of how similarly two languages structure their semantic clusters. We also introduce a new task, cluster-aware machine translation, which leverages cluster information to enhance translation quality. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we implemented both monolingual and multi-lingual pre-training models using our framework and evaluated them using our novel evaluation metric and a popular semantic similarity assessment tool. Our results show that both models' performance improves when using our framework, and they exhibit low cognitive difficulty levels when analyzed using the Flesch reading test. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Multi-Lingual-Shared-Semantic-Framework.

This paper presents measurements of pions, kaons, protons, and photons produced in Xe-Xe collisions at a 5.44 TeV collision energy. Many machine learning tasks involve a pair of training and testing distributions. In quality control, for example, models are often trained on data from different production lines or shifts, and then used to predict defects on unknown lines or shifts. In such cases, it is essential to account for distribution differences to ensure robust performance. In this paper, we investigate methods to improve the robustness of our proposed Discriminative Aggregation framework in federated settings. The framework aims to combine models from different entities based on their local data distributions in order to determine a single, high-quality model. We explore the connection between this task and classification, and introduce a new objective function that incorporates the Bayes factor ratio to ensure robust performance. We also examine the impact of robustness-enhancing techniques such as regularization and contrastive learning on model performance in federated settings. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating these techniques into the Discriminative Aggregation framework leads to significant improvements in quality control tasks. We further analyze and present methods to calculate the Bayes factor ratio, and show that regularized models tend to excel in situations with small distribution differences. Our research facilitates the use of the Discriminative Aggregation framework in various applications involving different training and testing distributions. Our code is available at https://github.com/lingwei-liu/Discriminative-FedAA.

The significance of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment is evaluated in a variety of scenarios that deviate from high-energy physics, including anomalous symmetry patterns, bundles that combine particles and forces, and string theories characterized by different Calabi-Yau landscapes. The magnitude to which such scenarios are sensitive to the tau's electric dipole moment is quantified by sensitivity coefficients, with contributions from various processes that involve the tau, its pair production, the $W$ boson and large missing energy, the $J/\psi$ meson, and the $\tau$ pair. The latter process, in particular, proves particularly informative as it directly involves the tau pair and thus provides a more precise measurement of the tau's electric dipole moment. Leveraging deep learning is crucial for automating information extraction from visually complex documents, but generating a large-scale labeled dataset for this purpose is a significant obstacle due to its high cost.  Our proposed approach, called Visual Document Data Augmentation (VDDA), combines synthetic full-page label modifications with partial label correction, allowing for significant reduction of labeling expenses.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of VDDA by incorporating it into a cycle-consistency guided segmentation framework, which can be applied to visually diverse documents containing financial information.  Our evaluation utilizes a newly assembled financial document dataset, consisting of 15,000 images with 5,000 labeled examples.  VDDA achieves a 2.4% relative improvement in F1-score compared to a baseline model trained on a minimally labeled dataset.  By adjusting labeling scopes, we show that VDDA can reduce labeling expenses by 87.5% while still outperforming baseline models.  Our proposed method is applicable to various visualization tasks and can be a valuable tool for conducting initial screening and prioritizing documents for manual label verification.  Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/vdda.

High-performance computing on GPUs requires efficient memory management on a large scale, which can be challenging due to limited memory resources, concurrent execution, and complex memory access patterns. Despite the advancement of automatic memory management through languages with object-based programming, developing large-scale GPU applications with popular object-based programming languages like CUDA-C, Metal, and DPC++ still faces significant memory management hurdles, particularly with memory allocation and access. In response to these limitations, we present DynaSOAr, a state-of-the-art, high-performance memory allocator tailored for object-based programming on GPUs. Featuring a novel, small object allocator with byte padding and fragmentation reduction, DynaSOAr combines concurrent safety, minimal performance overhead, and optimized memory usage. Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a large block allocator with streamlined configuration and advanced coalescing, which enhances memory access efficiency and reduces waste. By leveraging byte padding and optimized placement techniques, DynaSOAr achieves significant memory conservation and access efficiency, while also supporting dynamic memory configuration and tight integration with object-oriented programming features. In our evaluations, DynaSOAr demonstrates superior performance in various benchmarks and real-world applications, showcasing the potential of this memory allocator to handle the memory management challenges of object-based programming on GPUs. By conserving memory, enhancing data coalescing, and providing scalable concurrency, DynaSOAr achieves notable gains of 1.57 times, 2.55 times, and 3.30 times in memory allocation, execution speed, and combined performance, respectively, over popular open-source memory allocators. The DynaSOAr memory allocator is a versatile tool suitable for a broad range of GPU applications, from linear solvers and simulation tools to machine learning frameworks and real-time video encoding, which place a high priority on efficient memory management, minimal overhead, and object-oriented design. The source code for DynaSOAr is available under the permissive BSD license on GitHub at https://github.com/ArmadilloLibrary/DynaSOAr.

The non-equilibrium quantum dynamics of a qutrit lattice model, mimicking massive scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in (1+1)D, is investigated in this study. By applying a variety of quantum perturbation techniques to initial Gaussian states, we observe multiple distinct effects: the emergence of a convenient reference frame through amplitude scaling; the identification of critical points based on perturbed conformal field theory; and the relevance of trapped ions to this model. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of a proposal for a quantum simulator involving qutrits, assessing the condition under which the number of effective qudit dimensions remains sufficiently large to ensure reliable simulation accuracy. This evaluation is performed for two different perturbation approaches and it reveals that extremely narrow trapping modes are necessary, requiring sophisticated cooling techniques in order to ensure that the simulation is accurate. Nevertheless, this issue can be circumvented by expanding the simulator's space, effectively treating the simulation as if it were in the free field limit. Moreover, we discover that this model can be accurately simulated using a small number of trapped ions, possibly as low as three, depending on the specific implementation. This study was previously published in the Journal of Physics: Complexity.

This research develops a miniaturized temperature detector using 90nm transistors, enabling precise temperature measurements while considering process variations and voltage fluctuations. The design employs a 2-bit SAR ADC and a threshold-based comparison circuit, allowing it to determine the appropriate switch closure within a given temperature range. The temperature estimation formula used takes into account multiple source voltage levels, yielding a precision of 0.24 degrees Celsius. Furthermore, the design incorporates multiple reference temperatures across different voltage ranges, resulting in a 1.4 degrees Celsius error margin. This research paper focuses on two main concepts from geometry: Lie groupoids and stacks. Lie groupoids represent a non-abative generalization of Lie groups, while stacks capture the essence of Lie groups, taking into consideration their equivariant properties. By integrating geometric configurations found in the realm of Lie groups, we can define a category of algebraic objects called geometric configurations over Lie groupoids and stacks. Our primary goal is to establish an association between this category and the category of representations of the underlying groupoid. However, this association is not straightforward and depends on the particular groupoid in question. We find that this dependence results in the development of a Lie groupoid structure on the set of algebraic configurations, a phenomenon we can observe using stacks and specifically universal stacks, including bending transformations and Riemannian metrics. Furthermore, this notion extends to stacks that are locally stable under the action of Lie groups, allowing us to define configuration spaces that are invariant to these groups. This extension enables us to recover categories equivalent to the category of smooth objects under the action of these Lie groups. Our research also delves into the relationship between these configuration spaces and the groupoid in question, studying its properties and providing examples. A statistical analysis of 64 far-infrared dark filaments, spanning a range of masses, reveals that only the most massive ones, with masses greater than 30 times that of the sun, exhibit infrared darkness. This phenomenon can be explained by the absence of a bright infrared background in these areas due to massive gas blocks that lack embedded sources, likely resulting from the disintegration of protostellar cores. A study of a notable dragon-shaped infrared dark nebula, revealing massive gas blocks at its center, has led to the discovery of a massive protostar and a massive HII region on either side, surrounded by rapidly moving gas and dust, forming a massive colliding wind binary system unique in its type. This system, with a total mass equivalent to 60 times that of the sun, is remarkable for exhibiting both massive star formation and destruction, where massive molecules are being formed while dust is being dissipated, likely due to intense radiation and strong winds, and is comparable to the massive Pop III stars believed to have contributed to the early formation of the galaxy. This research suggests that massive infrared dark filaments, with masses greater than 30 times that of the sun, can give rise to both massive star formation and destruction, resulting in the death of the very stars that gave them birth. This is similar to the findings of a previous study on the Cygnus X complex, and provides a new perspective on the dynamic nature of massive star formation, and the role it plays in the surrounding environment, shaped by its own offspring. This is also reflected in the work of another researcher, who has identified similar infrared dark filaments surrounding the R136 and NGC 3603 star-forming regions, which are both characterized by massive star formation and destruction. This research has significant implications for the study of the early formation of the galaxy, and demonstrates that the death of massive stars is a necessary process for the formation of the elements that they give birth to, and that it is a self-destructive and necessary process for the creation of the elements and the formation of the galaxy itself. This is further reinforced by the findings of another study on the massive IR dark filaments in the Andromeda galaxy, the Milky Way, and the Centaurus A galaxy, which have revealed that these filaments have the necessary ingredients for both massive star formation and destruction, indicating that they have the necessary elements for creating metal and giving birth to death, and providing insight into the role of environment in shaping the formation and destruction of stars, and the distribution of elements and the formation

We establish one-step relations for the stochastic wave equation with rotationally symmetric noise on the sphere, specifically in three dimensions. These relations enable us to extend existing results from two-dimensional cases to their three-dimensional counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the stochastic wave equation on the sphere, with both the mean-square and $L^2$-norm definitions of solution applied. Additionally, we establish explicit expressions for one-step relations in the form of conditional expectations with respect to the noise, which can be used to derive explicit expectations and second-moment estimates for the solutions in three-dimensional scenarios. These results extend and generalize existing results for the planar case to the spherical case, specifically in three dimensions. Lastly, we provide a numerical example showcasing the accuracy of our results.

Complex liquid mixtures often exhibit varying levels of resistance to flow, a phenomenon that can be influenced by the interactions between different components and surface interactions with the container. In this study, we examine the surface tension and viscosity of bimodal liquid foams comprised of surfactant-free water and glycerol. Contrary to expectations, we find that the presence of water, which typically has a higher viscosity, can lead to an increase in the foam's resistance to flow due to its greater surface tension. This effect outweighs the impact of viscosity on the fluids' combined behavior. Our results demonstrate that the influence of surface tension can surpass that of viscosity in these systems and highlight the significance of interface hydrodynamics in governing flow resistance. Moreover, this study offers a practical approach for analyzing the resistance of liquid mixtures using a non-Newtonian model. Our findings also facilitate a deeper understanding of the dynamics of bimodal liquid foams and provide useful insights for optimizing the performance of containers with surface interactions. In addition, we demonstrate how the Rossler model can be applied to describe the flow of complex liquid systems, which may have far-reaching implications for related research topics. In the course of this study, we examined various glycerol-water combinations in addition to the initial bimodal foam sample, which included a water-alcohol mixture. Our data reveal that the presence of alcohol reduces the surface tension's influence on the foam's resistance to flow, largely counteracting its effect. On the other hand, our research indicates that the presence of water reduces the surface tension's impact on the foam's resistance to flow when it is combined with a non-surfactant oil. In both cases, the resistance to flow can be accurately represented by a power-law model that takes into account the average viscosity of the mixture. However, when water is the component, the model indicates that the resistance to flow is more resistant to change, which may be attributed to its greater surface tension. In contrast, when alcohol is the component, the model shows that the resistance to flow becomes more sensitive to changes, which may be caused by alcohol's lower surface tension compared to water. The detection of cancerous cells is crucial, and doctors rely on histopathology images to diagnose skin carcinoma. However, identifying these images can be difficult and time-consuming due to the intricate details and similar appearances between cancerous and benign cells. In addition to challenges faced by medical professionals, there are also difficulties in accurately classifying images in dermatology clinics. Modern machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, have successfully been applied to dermatology image analysis by extracting complex features from images. In addition to its success, the proposed method also incorporates an approach to treat noisy data, which is a realistic representation of actual image data, helping us evaluate the method's performance on certain levels of image noise, representing how the method handles normal variability in images and can also identify abnormal images. We tested the method on two datasets of skin carcinoma images and found it to be highly effective in not only determining the type of cell but also in detecting noisy images, which we considered to represent images taken during dermoscopy. The method's performance was comparable to or better than other state-of-the-art techniques. We believe this method has significant potential for use in clinical settings due to its simplicity and ability to handle noisy images. In addition to skin carcinoma, it can be applied to images in other fields such as breast cancer, colon cancer, lung cancer, etc. The method is also suitable for use on other images with similar classification problems. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghasemipourGhasemi/DCN_NN_Dermoscopy.git. The method's performance on two datasets of skin carcinoma images is available in the additional files at http://www.bmi.rug.nl/nipso2018/index.php?paper=123. The method's performance on noisy images after the conference was tested on a third dataset of skin carcinoma images and the results are available in the additional files at http://www.bmi.rug.nl/nipso2018/index.php?paper=123. The method's performance on another dataset of lung cancer images is available in the additional files at http://www.bmi.rug.nl/nipso2018/index.php?paper=123. The method's performance on another dataset of colon cancer images is available in the additional files at http://www.bmi.rug.nl/nipso2018/index.php?paper=123. The method's performance on another dataset of breast cancer images is available in the additional files at http://www.bmi.rug.nl/nipso2018/index.php

The behavior of a advancing interface in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell with low viscosity liquid displacing a more viscous liquid is examined, and we find that the interface's directionality can be effectively described by a variable flexibility metric. This metric depends on the angular velocity of the cell and the viscosity ratio between the two liquids. When the cell rotates rapidly, the interface's directionality becomes highly non-linear, and the interface takes on a cusp-like shape, even when there is a small difference in viscosity between the two liquids. This cusp shape leads to a sticky boundary phenomenon, where the interface becomes trapped at a 180-degree reversal in direction, following an initial displacement. This occurs even when the rotation speed slows down, where the interface refills slowly, but remains stuck at the cusp shape until it reaches the original position. This process can happen multiple times along the same interface, depending on the cell's rotation speed and the viscosity ratio between the two liquids. This phenomenon is so persistent that it leaves an persistent memory of its own, where the interface becomes trapped at any 180-degree reversal in direction, even if the cell's rotation speed slows down. This persistent memory of the interface can also be seen in a static scenario, where there are multiple 180-degree boundary reversals along the same interface, and it requires a significant increase in the cell's rotation speed to change the interface's direction, resulting in a curved interface. This curvature can also result in a sticky interface in a static scenario, where the interface becomes trapped at any change in direction, not limited to 180 degrees, and it takes a significant increase in the cell's rotation speed to change the interface's direction, where the interface refills slowly, but remains stuck at the curved shape until it reaches the original position. This persistent memory of the interface's directionality can be changed by increasing the cell's rotation speed to a point where the interface breaks curve, and it starts to change direction quickly, but this requires a different set of conditions for each interface shape. This phenomenon of a sticky and curved interface that has memory of its own has been theoretically predicted, but this study proves it happens in a Hele-Shaw cell, and it opens up a new field of investigation in nonlinear dynamics. Scientists first discovered the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecule in space, specifically in the TMC-1 cloud, through radio astronomical observations, and attributed its presence to cylic C-C triple bond formations due to lack of alternative explanations. A deeper analysis of the spectral data reveals the existence of two distinct isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, as well as variants involving the substitution of C-C triple bonds with C-N bonds, which have been previously undetected, except for the already known cyclopentadienyl cyanide. A comparative study of the measured molecular values with astrophysical models reveals that the two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene have similar amounts, and the CCH and CN variant ratios are nearly the same, however the total amount of ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its cyanogen analogue does appear to be greater than the sum of the two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene. A connection between these molecular variations and the possible physical conditions of the TMC-1 cloud is also explored. A note is made about the relatively precise measurement of the rotational constant for the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecule, which may be useful for future laboratory experiments aimed at comparing measured and simulated spectral outcomes. A thorough examination of the detected molecular quantities across various astronomical sources reveals that ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its cyanogen analogue do exist in other clouds, including Sgr B2, Orion KL, and Vela C, with the exception of DR21(OH), and with variations in the CCH and CN variant ratios of these molecules. A comparison is made between the measured molecular quantities and astrophysical models of different cloud environments, and the most likely formation pathways for these molecules are discussed, with chemical route sequences mapped out, along with an analysis of the detected molecular variations across these sources. A search for related molecules, such as cyclopentadienyl acetylene, cyclopentadienyl methylacetylene, and pentadienyl cyanide, yields detectable signal levels only for the latter in the TMC-1 cloud, with no detection of the former in any of the surveyed clouds, and with no evidence of the latter in Sgr B2, Orion KL, and Vela C. A discussion is presented on the importance of ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its isomers, and the possible connection between the presence of these molecules and the formation of larger hydrocarbon cycles

Recent advances in neural machine translation have led to the development of attention-based models, which enable the focus on specific parts of the input array to produce more accurate translation results. Building on this work, researchers have explored methods for using attention-based models in machine interpretation creation, such as text summarization. However, current approaches typically limit the focus to the immediate context, without considering future creation processes. In this paper, a new method called Look-ahead Focus for Creation in Neural Machine Interpretation is presented, which utilizes the forecast of the creation process and the difference between the forecast and the current input to guide the focus, resulting in higher quality outputs and, as demonstrated, improved performance in various creation tasks. The proposed approach outperforms existing benchmarks in several evaluation metrics, including the BLEU score, CIDEr, and RO-bleu, in tasks like neural machine translation, abstractive summarization, and chatbot development. The proposed approach also reduces the difficulty of training the model and prevents the focus from becoming overly complex. The proposed code is available at https://github.com/ghru/look-ahead-focus.

The experience of Scientific Grid Workflow Engines developed in Europe being successfully implemented in India, a culturally and linguistically distinct country, is examined in this research. An approach called the Translational Research Framework, which facilitates the adaptation and application of complex systems across different environments, is illustrated through this case study. The challenges encountered during the project, such as managing complex datasets, handling linguistic and terrestrial barriers, and maintaining data privacy, are addressed in the development of the grid computing framework, specifically the Grid Workflow Engine. A comparison with established grid computing platforms, along with performance benchmarks and real-world deployments, demonstrates the effectiveness of this translatable approach, a concept that can be applied to other development projects involving Indian contexts or similar translational scenarios. The open-source code of the Grid Workflow Engine is available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/HealthGrid/GridWorkflowEngine. The research behind this paper was previously published in proceedings from various conferences, as listed in the appendix. The current paper provides a comprehensive examination of the experience, the translatable approach, and the engine's performance, presenting new information that supplements the original research findings. This model exhibits unique properties, such as a point mass and no long-range force, and its dissipative component breaks the Lorentz invariance. A scalar field model with a mass term was historically associated with cosmological constants. Now, with the combined model, we find that it can describe the acceleration of the universe in its early stages. Furthermore, it has a solution that matches the de Sitter space in the early stages of the universe, and it has the potential to provide a point mass gravitational effect similar to that caused by dark matter. The combined model also offers insights into the fundamental nature of space and time, and it suggests that the concept of space and time may need to be reexamined. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light neutrinos and dark energy. We analyze the J/ψ decay width and demonstrate that, due to its small value, it can be an appropriate standard for rare processes. We also calculate the J/ψ decay width into light neutrinos and determine the accessible energy ranges for the process. Furthermore, we determine the J/ψ decay width into the "invisible" process, which represents the sum of the light neutrino and two-photons decay processes. We then utilize these findings to derive constraints on rare electron decays and the energy range of dark energy. These constraints originate from the efficient suppression of the J/ψ invisible decay width into light neutrinos and two photons due to its similarity in form to the efficient field theories of neutrino and dark energy. These constraints take the forms of an upper limit on the rare electron decay rate and the energy range of dark energy, which vary with the dark energy parameter and reach their maximum values for certain values of this parameter where they become independent of the dark energy mass. We then compare these constraints with existing limits obtained from other processes and experiments and also with the energy scales of effective field theories. We further analyze the contributions of different light neutrino flavors to the J/ψ invisible decay width and the effects of assuming that the light neutrino sum represents the sum of the absolute values of the individual neutrino flavors rather than their squares. We also investigate the implications of these assumptions for the constraints on rare electron decays and dark energy and the energy scales of effective field theories. We further analyze the J/ψ electron pair production at a collider and its connection to the efficient field theories of neutrino and dark energy. We also investigate the access to the light neutrino mass spectrum and the dark sector parameter through the J/ψ system at a collider and the effects of assuming that the light neutrino sum represents the sum of the absolute values of the individual neutrino flavors rather than their squares. We derive these quantities for the case where the light neutrino sum represents the sum of the absolute values of the individual neutrino flavors and determine the relevant energy range for this case. We further analyze the efficiency of this process in constraining the light neutrino mass spectrum and the dark sector parameter and the energy ranges for which this process is effective in this case. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) variations, incorporating singular spectrum analysis (SSA) into multivariate functional time series (MFTS) research. Building on the foundation of MFSSA, we develop MFSSA for use in variable-dimensional domains. Further developments lead to Multivariate Functional Multi-Singular Spectrum Analysis (MFMSA), whose properties are studied and a hybrid approach is presented. Both of these variants' performance is evaluated in a range of scenarios, including real-world applications. The results show that the proposed methods outperform the baseline in a range of scenarios. The implementation of these methods in R is also provided. The research highlights potential uses for MFSSA and MFMSA, while also highlighting potential areas for future development, including the integration of MFMSA with multivariate functional forecasting methods. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a random walk in one dimension, where the walk is subject to changes in speed that follow a general distribution, depending on the time frame. We establish general conditions under which the duration of the walk within a specific region remains finite for almost all realizations, without regard to the magnitude of the underlying parameter that defines the walk's boundary. In addition to this result, we establish that there is a critical parameter threshold such that the duration of the walk is finite for almost all realizations when the underlying parameter falls below this threshold, without regard to the magnitude of the parameter that defines the walk's boundary. This latter result extends the findings of [1, Theorem 1] to walks bounded on one side. Moreover, we provide specific conditions that can be applied to walk speeds that follow a mixture of subexponential distributions, yielding explicit lower bounds on the walk's duration for almost all realizations. Finally, we provide numerical evidence for random walk speeds distributed as a shifted gamma distribution, as well as an analytical characterization of the walk's survival probability in this setting. This research was conducted in collaboration with S. M. N. S. Rui, whose contributions are acknowledged. The findings presented in this paper were previously published in the journal Applied Mathematics and Optimization, volume 77, issue 3, pages 271-307, 2019, under the title "On the Recurrence of Random Walks with Time-Dependent Speed in One Dimension" by S. M. N. S. Rui and A. A. Youssef. The current research extends those results in [2, Theorems 1 and 2] to walks bounded on both sides. In addition to [2], this research also builds upon the papers Random Walk with Constant Speed in a Convex Domain by A. G. Alves, B. F. Mattos, and Y. O. B. Vasconcellos, and Random Walk in a Convex Domain with Changing Speed by A. G. Alves, B. F. Mattos, Y. O. B. Vasconcellos, and T. J. Wooley, which are cited accordingly. The IShTAR plasma generator at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics has been characterized to simulate and match its plasma parameters to those in the edge plasma of the ITER device. A new model incorporating a helicon source has been developed and shows that in the IShTAR device, a helicon regime exists at lower power levels, and it matches the experimental data. However, due to limited access to the generator's physical details, some assumptions had to be made in the model, which could affect the accuracy of the results. A comparison with other plasma parameters measured in the experiment showed that they match the model well, except for the degree of plasma turbulence and some plasma fluctuations. Further development of the model could help in better understanding the plasma dynamics in the generator. A helicon regime is considered important for developing a plasma scan technique that could be used in the edge plasma of ITER. A discussion on the feasibility of this technique is included. A plasma scan technique could be used to map the plasma parameters across the plasma boundary of ITER, which is essential for evaluating the quality of its plasma boundary diversion system. A discussion is also included on the characteristics of the plasma fluctuations that occur in the helicon regime of the IShTAR generator, which could be related to fluctuations that occur in the edge plasma of ITER. A comparison with another plasma source, the CAPRICOI generator, that has a similar design to the IShTAR generator but with some differences, shows that both generators have a helicon regime but at different power levels, which could be related to the differences in their design. A discussion is included on the factors that could be influencing the fluctuations in the LPA-2000 bean.
