While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting cancer cells from images across various types of cancers. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that is capable of performing high-quality nucleus segmentation on histopathology images automatically. The proposed network yields superior results in relation to widely-used evaluation metrics and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple cancer types. The data used in this study comprises 50 images from the CVC-Colon Cancer Detection Dataset, 50 images from the NDIA Dataset, and 50 images from the CVC-07 Dataset. The proposed network has also been applied to a real-world application, the automatic visualization of cancer cells for a particular type of lung cancer. The code for the proposed network has been made publicly available on a well-known open-source platform. The results obtained have been compared to those of two widely-used baseline methods, U-Net and ATTER-Net, and show significant improvements in evaluation metrics such as the Dice Coefficient and the Hausdorff Distance. The proposed network has the potential to be a high-performance, automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of extracting cancer cells from images across various types of cancers. The results obtained have been further analyzed and the areas that require improvement have been identified. Let's consider a local, non-abelian field extension K/Qv for a p-adic village V, where p is an odd prime number. We establish a regional converse theorem for the special orthogonal groups in degree 2n, with n being an odd number greater than 1, and the classical symplectic groups in degree 2n, with n being an even number greater than 1, for a Galois group G arising from the extension K/Qv. Specifically, this result holds under the assumption that S_n is not a subgroup of G and certain local integral twist minimization conditions are met. Our conclusion then states that a non-trivial element sigma of G is not contained within the subgroup of G generated by the Galois groups associated with (non-trivial) Frobenius elements lambda_i, each linked to a pair of isogenies theta_i and psi_i of certain specified types. We also investigate how our finding extends to global, algebraic extensions. Deep Neural Network technology has seen significant progress in recent years.
Within the realm of graph-based data analysis, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks
have emerged as particularly useful tools. We focus on the most well-known GCNN
variants: Graph Convolutional Layer (GCL) and Graph Attention Layer (GAT). Our
investigations aim to gain a deeper understanding of these networks by examining
their relationship to traditional signal processing concepts. Specifically, we
reveal that GCL and GAT can be interpreted through the lens of matched filtering
principles. Our analysis highlights a crucial insight: both GCL and GAT equations
can be seen as implementations of matched filtering, using local feature spectra
as our reference. We further derive an optimization problem for GAT, using the
matched filtering criterion. This approach allows us to introduce a new loss
function, which we call the Spectral Matching Loss (SML). We propose and evaluate
SML on multiple datasets, and our results show that it outperforms the standard
GAT loss functions. We also provide a code repository to facilitate further
research based on our insights. Our analysis provides researchers with a unique
perspective on the underlying principles of GCNNs, and our derivations offer a
way to explore more efficient and effective network designs. We hope this study
will lead to new insights and new methodologies in the field of GCNNs. We also
believe that our signal processing-oriented perspective on GCNNs provides a
foundation for investigating other complex machine learning models. Our code is
available at: https://github.com/ghrasoul/Spectral-Matching-Layer. Our research

This alternative formulation leads to a conformally invariant expression for the Chern-Simons action, which can be used to describe the spinning soliton phase, as proven through numerical solutions of the field equations. Additionally, an analytical representation of the soliton solution is derived for a specific group, demonstrating that the Chern-Simons action is capable of producing spinning soliton solutions in two-dimensional spacetime. A key finding associated with this model is that there are two distinct solutions for the black hole equation of state, an interesting result that contrasts with the conventional hypothesis of a unique solution for this equation in two-dimensional spacetime. In five-dimensional spacetime, the model based on the Chern-Simons action allows for the existence of a black hole solution with a hypersurface boundary condition, which can be confirmed through direct calculation of the entropy associated with this black hole solution. The spin-dependent interaction terms inherent to this model also lead to intriguing results regarding the soliton solution, which now incorporates spin-dependent interaction effects that influence the soliton's structure. Moreover, the model based on the Chern-Simons action enables the derivation of the conformal factor's expression, which in turn allows for the interpretation of the soliton solution in terms of spin-dependent interaction effects. The model based on the Chern-Simons action's stability is associated with the conserved current's nature, which can be confirmed through the calculation of the soliton solution's mass and pressure gradients in the soliton solution case, as well as the temperature and energy density in the black hole solution case. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. However, precision is often compromised due to limited access to patients' full side views resulting from the curved surface of transducers. This research introduces the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method to enhance the accuracy of lateral shift estimations, a critical step in elastography, by generating synthetic arrays that conform to the shape of transducers. Lateral shift is determined by cross-correlation of synthetic data with real data, and multiple combinations of VOSA arrays and real data are combined to improve precision. This technique has been tested on numerical models and phantom data, with the results demonstrating a significant improvement in precision to half pixel in ideal conditions. Furthermore, its applicability has been demonstrated on real-time two-dimensional elastography of rabbit muscles during surgery. This novel approach is suitable for a wide range of transducers, including elastography transducers used in the 2D and 3D systems. This research was conducted at the University of British Columbia. The VOSA method has been made available online for public use. The proposed technique offers a non-contact method of estimating the distance between transducers and tissues, with applications extending to the imaging of tissues with complex surface geometries. The challenges faced in the development of this method serve as valuable lessons for the advancement of ultrasound imaging technologies. The proposed algorithm can be integrated into real-time elastography systems for clinical use, with potential users including researchers and medical professionals. Humans excel at understanding code written in traditional programming languages, thanks to the widespread use of programming. However, the high incidence of debugging issues limits the efficiency of code-based teaching. In contrast, demonstrating algorithms on interactive calculators is remarkably effective in ensuring concept comprehension. To bridge this gap, we propose a new concept - a specification for algorithms that we call 'rational pseudocodes,' which can be understood by both humans and automated proof systems. We show that rational pseudocodes can be linked to interactive demonstrations, providing solid grounds for validating the correctness of algorithms. Furthermore, this connection enables an assessment of the precision of human-implemented algorithms. We demonstrate this approach with renowned algorithms, including binary search and sorting, and analyze the associated validation proofs in depth. Although this approach generates intricate proofs, we observe that these proofs mirror the complex reasoning underlying human implementations of the algorithms. In a separate experiment, we found that this method can also be applied to teaching, where it delivers engaging interactive demonstrations from a wide range of algorithms written in rational pseudocode. We make our rational pseudocode specification available under the Creative Commons license. In its present form, this definition serves as a foundation that other researchers can extend and refine. We encourage them to explore this idea further and provide a definition that enables the automatic translation of rational pseudocodes into a form that can be executed by various platforms, including robotic arms, by leveraging existing translation technologies. In a broader context, this approach falls under the category of specifications that define tasks that involve reasoning, and provides a new perspective on the debate surrounding the nature of tasks and their corresponding representations. In addition, this method provides a means of implementing the idea of teaching algorithms in a more abstract form, as originally proposed by Alan Turing. We believe that this approach has vast potential for application in various fields, including but not limited to education, AI development, and technology-based learning, and we are willing to collaborate with other researchers, educators, and technology experts who share our interests and can benefit from this concept. In the context of dynamic data streams, the task is to maintain a summary of input points grouped into $k$ clusters based on their proximity to center points, with the goal of identifying points that belong to specific clusters. Building on previous work, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm to efficiently compute a representative subset of input points that accurately reflects the structure of the input data, enabling the effective determination of cluster members. Our algorithm achieves near-optimal performance in terms of subset size and clustering error, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving large numbers of input dimensions. Specifically, in the standard Euclidean space, our algorithm produces a coreset of input points with a size of $O(k \cdot \log^2 d)$ within $O(k \cdot \log^2 d \cdot (n + poly(d)))$ storage, compared to the optimal size of $O(k \cdot \log d)$ and surpassing the performance of existing methods in terms of storage requirement. Furthermore, our algorithm yields a storage-based guarantee for the space utilization, achieving a distinction among existing coreset-based clustering solutions. Moreover, we develop a batch version of our algorithm, which enables efficient update of the coreset in response to incoming data points, thereby reducing the computational complexity associated with the task of determining cluster membership for each point. We thoroughly evaluate the performance of our algorithm through extensive experimental trials, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods in scenarios involving intricate data configurations and complex high-dimensional data. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on state division to prevent contraction, our method tackles the challenge of dividing the game state into hierarchical sections that maximize the level of confrontation. Our research reveals that strategy-based pursuit-withdrawal games can be effectively divided into hierarchical sections using a state division approach, which enables efficient solution deployment through multi-level representation. To support this finding, we establish a key theorem that facilitates division based on reward and transition functions. Furthermore, this research is applied to hierarchical reinforcement learning settings, which enhances the efficacy of learning by limiting the exploration to a shorter hierarchy. To validate our results, we present a real-world example involving hierarchical reinforcement learning. Additionally, we outline an illustrative algorithm to demonstrate the practical feasibility of our approach. By offering a precise and efficient solution to hierarchical division, our method provides a valuable insight into the complex structure of stochastic pursuit-withdrawal games. This research focuses on developing an efficient method for detecting vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon collisions. Due to the vast amount of data involved, a fast vector boson estimation approach is crucial for historical muon data. To achieve this, we propose two alternative methods to determine the direction of vector bosons based on missing transverse energy, utilizing either a single longitdinal detector plane or a pair of zero-degree thin gap detectors. Lepton flavor vulnerability and fake generation suppression are key aspects of both proposals. We also explore two algorithms to establish vector boson properties: a simple, fast'maximum likelihood' approach and a more accurate 'kernel density estimation' method. To validate these ideas, we utilized ATLAS zero-degree detector simulation data and missing transverse energy responses, leveraging muon reconstruction tools for ATLAS. These developments are utilized in two scenarios: (1) fast vector boson estimation for same-flavor lepton pairs, and (2) efficient kernel density estimation for different lepton flavor pairs. We further investigate ways to enhance efficiency and accuracy, such as utilizing muon momenta, correcting for detector effects, and exploring alternative density estimation techniques. Despite the advancement of model-based reinforcement learning, this method often results in slow learning processes. Our research focuses on accelerating the development of modular systems with separate control and learning components in a simulated environment where a virtual robot navigates and completes various tasks. Our findings, confirmed by both an independent animator and a sophisticated simulation featuring physical interactions, reveal that modular systems significantly boost the rate at which important skills are developed and significantly reduce the risk of severe setbacks during critical operations. Our results also demonstrate that modular systems excel in comparison to non-modular alternatives, demonstrating a substantial difference in critical areas. Furthermore, our research highlights the presence of an optimal balance between the level of sophistication within the predictive model and its computational efficiency, a factor that significantly impacts performance. In situations where measurements are affected by a distorted or degraded medium, inverse problems in physics and engineering pose significant challenges. These difficulties arise especially when the medium that caused the distortion is unknown or complexly structured, categorizing them as an inverse problem of multi-parameter screening in a highly noisy environment. A common approach to addressing this problem is to treat it as a classification problem, but such methods fail to utilize the underlying continuity of the forward problem to their advantage. A better strategy involves developing algorithms that incorporate the smooth nature of the problem, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy of the solutions. In this research, we introduce a novel architecture based on conditional generators, incorporates both regularized and conditional elements to achieve highly accurate results with the added benefit of reducing the data required for training by half. A numerical experiment using a highly noisy dataset shows that our innovation significantly enhances the precision of the solutions, a finding that is also theoretically supported. In addition to that, we discover that the proposed architecture has the capability of handling a more complicated scenario where the measurements are distorted by two unknown layers, a finding that is also demonstrated through numerical data. A simplified and a deep learning-based approach to solve this problem are presented, with the latter showing a much more accurate result. The proposed regularized conditional generator can be applied to other problems of screening multi-parameter targets or objects in noisy environments, such as in medical imaging, remote sensing, and seismic exploration. A general discussion on the different challenges and approaches to solving forward and reverse problems and on the proposed architecture is provided in the concluding section. A regularized conditional generator can also be referred to as a modified version of the cGAN architecture, with the terms such as smooth source, smooth target, smooth source mapping, and smooth target mapping being used interchangeably. The challenge of detecting the smooth target or source in imaging problems can be formulated as a classification, segmentation, or reverse problem, with different levels of complexity and solutions such as traditional, deep learning-based, or combination-based methods being employed. Despite the added benefit of continuous regularization on the accuracy of the solutions, this research also shows that the quality of the proxy dataset generated through backward sampling has a significant impact on the accuracy of the solutions, with two different numerical experiments showing that there are various ways to improve this quality including the addition of noise to the measurements, using a more complex generator network, and modifying the forward problem, with the result of the experiment showing that there is a certain level of threshold on the level of noise that can be added to the measurements before the quality of the solutions

The interstellar medium is home to a vast network of interstellar clouds and streams that surround the solar system. These objects, which include molecular clouds, stellar streams, and interstellar gas and dust, influence the propagation of electromagnetic waves emitted by pulsars. Pulsar scintillation, a phenomenon caused by the interaction between pulsar emission and dense interstellar matter, can be used to map the complex structure of the surrounding medium. A thorough analysis of the scintillation patterns of the bright pulsar B1133+16 over the course of nearly four decades has uncovered evidence of a dense interstellar cloud along the line of sight to this pulsar. A super-resolution reconstruction of the scintillation patterns as they change over time reveals a large, smooth gradient indicating the presence of this cloud. Furthermore, a comparison of the scintillation patterns in the time-domain and the spatial structure of the pulsar beam allows for the inference of the cloud's physical characteristics, including its length, width, and depth. A super-resolution reconstruction of the electron column density within the line of sight to B1133+16 reveals an overall density gradient as well as localized, discrete streams and clouds. These findings are consistent with the presence of a molecular cloud located at a distance of approximately 5.6 parsecs from the solar system, and streams and clouds located at greater distances. A further comparison with the dust and gas maps of the Milky Way adds to the understanding of this complex environment, and highlights the dynamic and variable nature of the interstellar medium. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach and pitched-controlled audio with pitch-sensitive diluted convolution layers. To further investigate the frame rate's effect on model performance, this study conducts experiments with various frame rates, demonstrating that higher frame rates yield better results, especially for larger model sizes. The proposed QPNet, using a 10-frame dilation pattern, delivers generated audio with an average score of 0.444 for the Mean Opinion Score (MOS), outperforming WN by 0.053, and the state-of-the-art Griffin-Lim method by 0.063, while maintaining reasonable computational complexity. Moreover, QPNet exhibits superior quality when compared to WN and the current speech generation models, specifically in voices with clear formant structures. The proposed model's performance is further validated through synthesis of the VCTK corpus, demonstrating its broad applicability in a variety of voice genres. The bicategorical invariants theory has its foundations rooted in the theory of subfields within the extension fields, as identified by Galois group actions on fields. Extending these concepts to the realm of shadows, we define the shadows of a field with respect to a Galois extension. It is then demonstrated that the shadows retain the property of being marked within the shadow structure, thus establishing a direct connection to the original field. Furthermore, we establish that the shadows can be unified under the umbrella of a unified shadow structure, specifically the quotient of the shadow structure by the action of the Galois group. This unified shadow structure contains the marks of the original field, and it possesses a unique property where it is invariant to the action of the Galois group. This leads to the discovery of the shadows that are associated with the generic field structure, which can be viewed as the shadows of the field itself. This in turn allows us to reinterpret the associated functors as being equivalent to the functor of the shadow structure, with the action of the Galois group being autonomous. For individuals who are deaf or hard-of-hearing, auditory communication is severely impaired, affecting their ability to navigate safely within their environment. To address this issue, a method is proposed to determine the origin of sounds emanating from a 3D space, without relying on visual cues or head-related signals, by using wearable technology consisting of microphones placed behind the ears. By utilizing a level set approach and machine learning, the method localizes sounds in 3D space on a per-frame basis, while the level set algorithm tracks the sound's origin over time, resulting in an average accuracy of 84.5% in guessing the sound's 3D direction 1 second into the recording, and 87.1% 2 seconds into the recording. Furthermore, the method demonstrates high efficiency, requiring minimal computational resources. The technology has been applied in realistic scenarios, including at home and in public spaces, with results showing it can be effective for certain environments while struggling with noisy conditions and complex sound scenarios. The method's limitations also prompt ideas for its expansion, such as integrating head-related signals, treating multiple simultaneous sounds, and improving performance in noisy environments, all of which could enhance its utility further. The underlying methodology is flexible and can be adapted for other applications, such as sound source analysis in robotics, by integrating the level set algorithm with other methods, such as differential evolution algorithms. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by their application in representing complex and non-euclidean data, a trait that makes GNNs a promising choice for various difficult-to-annotate datasets. Despite the promising results, a significant issue with GNNs remains their reliance on Euclidean metrics, specifically the use of Euclidean distances in various learning tasks. This limitation becomes particularly problematic when GNNs are applied to data that cannot be represented in Euclidean space, such as graphs based on genetic relationships, semantic EMRs, and organizational networks. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel concept of a Lorentzian GNN that utilizes the principles of Lorentzian geometry to define network structures and learning methods based on the metric. Unlike traditional GNNs that rely on Euclidean distances, Lorentzian GNNs provide multiple benefits, including the automatic generation of network attributes, the reduction of required annotation, and robust performance in various learning tasks. Additionally, Lorentzian GNNs offer a more precise understanding of network properties and can be applied to a wide range of tasks, from classification to generation, without the need for additional annotation. A software implementation of Lorentzian GNN is available at https://github.com/alireza-convolution/Lorentzian-GNN.

Reconstructing acoustic structures and their attached components from recorded sound waves is a complex problem with many possible solutions. However, for many applications, it's not enough to simply recover the underlying geometry, but rather to determine the precise properties of the structure, the component, the medium, and how they interact with each other. This challenge becomes even more complex when the data available is limited, as is the case with inverse problems. This study presents a novel approach to addressing this challenging problem by leveraging a hybrid method that combines geometric and analytical techniques. Specifically, it uses a geometric algorithm to recover a preliminary structure, which is then refined using an analytical method that takes into account the properties of the components and the acoustic equation. This hybrid approach is demonstrated on a synthetic model featuring a thin plate and a cylindrical cavity, as well as on actual data representing a metal plate and human voice, with the results showing that it can effectively recover the structure, the component, and the medium, and even determine the boundary conditions of the problem. Furthermore, it highlights the risk of multiple solutions and offers an approach to handle it, as well as provides an interpretation of the recovered interaction operator that reflects the unique characteristics of the problem being studied. This research also involves an experimental demonstration of a sound-structure interaction using a vocalized cylindrical cavity, with the results showing that it can recover the shape and size of the cavity, as well as provide an estimation of the boundary conditions and the interaction operator, and even detect minor modifications to the cavity. This study's findings serve as a foundation for further advancements in sound structure interaction, including a related problem that involves determining the properties of a structure based on the sounds it produces. This approach's efficiency has been validated on actual data representing a plate and a human voice, with the results showing that it can recover the shape, size, and properties of the structure, as well as provide an estimation of the interaction operator, and even detect minor modifications to the structure.
